opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest shift for me was realizing how much we take the multilayer perceptron for granted. For decades it's been the default building block, and most innovation has happened on top of it: attention, convolutions, normalization tricks. When we started working on KANs, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, the question was almost naive: what if we put the learnable nonlinearity on the edges instead of fixed activation functions on the nodes? Once you ask that, you see that the basic building blocks themselves are a design choice, not a law of nature.

The second thing it changed is how I think about interpretability. With an MLP you usually train first and then try to reverse-engineer what the network learned, which is very hard. With KANs, each edge is a one-dimensional function you can plot. So you can look at it, prune it, and sometimes even recognize it, like "oh, this looks like a sine" or "this looks quadratic," and snap it to a symbolic form. That made me believe interpretability shouldn't only be a post-hoc analysis. It can be built into the architecture from the start, so the model is easier for humans to collaborate with.

That connects to the third point, which is about what AI is for, especially in science. If the goal is only to maximize benchmark accuracy on huge datasets, then scale and hardware efficiency dominate, and honestly MLPs and transformers are extremely well optimized for GPUs. KANs aren't always the right tool there. But in scientific settings you often care about getting a compact, understandable formula, or discovering structure, or putting your domain knowledge back into the model. There, an architecture whose inductive biases match the problem, like smoothness and compositional structure, can matter more than raw scale.

So overall I came away thinking about architecture design as being less about one universal winner and more about matching the inductive biases to the problem and the user. I'd also include the human in the loop as part of the design. And I became more comfortable questioning the foundations. Sometimes the most interesting ideas come from revisiting something everyone assumed was settled. The Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem was considered kind of useless for machine learning for a long time, and it turned out there was still something there when we looked at it from a different angle.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest change wasn't technical at all. It was realizing how much of what we treat as "settled" in deep learning is really just historical accident.

When we started KAN, the idea was almost embarrassingly simple. MLPs put fixed activation functions on the nodes and learn the weights on the edges. We just flipped it: put learnable functions on the edges, and sum at the nodes. That's the whole thing. And it comes from a theorem that's been around since the 1950s, the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem. People had looked at it before and dismissed it, mostly because the original theorem gives you these pathological, non-smooth functions that look useless in practice. What we did was let go of the exact theorem and treat it as inspiration instead of a constraint. Once you allow deeper and wider networks, the pathologies go away.

So the first lesson for me was: don't be too reverent toward the theory, but also don't be too reverent toward the status quo. Both can trap you.

The second thing is that I stopped thinking of architecture as something you optimize purely for benchmark numbers. I come from physics, and what I actually want from a model is something I can read. With KAN, after training you can look at each edge, see that this one became a sine, that one became x squared, prune the rest, and sometimes you can literally write down the formula the network discovered. That changed my sense of what "a good architecture" means. For AI for science, interpretability isn't a nice-to-have you bolt on at the end. It has to be built into the structure, because the scientist and the model need to be able to collaborate. The human brings priors, the model brings fitting power, and the architecture should be the interface between them.

And the third change, which I think about a lot now, is that different problems want different inductive biases. For language and vision, MLPs and transformers are great, and I'm not claiming KAN will replace them. But for small, scientific, low-dimensional problems where the ground truth is often compositional and smooth, a spline-based edge function is simply a better prior. So instead of asking "what is the one architecture," I started asking "what is the right architecture for this type of structure in the data." It sounds obvious, but the field's momentum pushes very hard toward one universal recipe.

I also became more humble about how to evaluate things. When KAN came out, there were people who were overly excited and people who were overly dismissive, and both were kind of reacting to the hype rather than the object. The real answer is boring: it's a tool, it's good at some things, worse at others, and the interesting question is to characterize that boundary carefully. Developing it taught me that an architecture is not a product, it's more like a hypothesis about the world. You propose it, and then you let the problems tell you where it's right.

astra-6.text:
It made me think more carefully about what we build into an architecture and what we allow it to learn. There’s always a tradeoff: too much structure can restrict the model, but too little structure can make learning inefficient and the result hard to understand.

For me, the interesting question is whether we can choose a structure that makes useful patterns easier to discover—and easier for us to inspect afterward. Especially for scientific problems, getting an accurate prediction is only part of the goal. We also want to learn something from the model.

So I would frame architecture design less as finding one universal architecture and more as choosing the right assumptions for the problem. What relationships should the model represent naturally? What should be learnable? And can we understand what it learned? Those questions matter alongside scale and benchmark performance.

sol-6.1.text:
It made me think of architecture less as a fixed structure that we ask learning to compensate for, and more as a hypothesis about how a problem should be represented. The architecture itself is an inductive bias: it makes some solutions easy to discover and others very difficult.

So the question becomes, what should we build in, and what should we allow the model to learn? Too much structure can limit discovery, but too little can make learning inefficient and the result hard to understand. For me, the interesting direction is to make those choices explicit and testable—to design models that can help us understand why they work, as well as produce good predictions.
